title: KAKE NEWS INVESTIGATES: Duplicate license plate numbers lead to dangerous situations for some Kansas drivers

reading.body:
The failure is a match on an identifier that is not unique. Flock cameras read only the letters and numbers on a plate, not the background, and Kansas reuses the same numbers across different plate designs. The Spurlocks' KU Alumni plate 7007 and a temporary Kansas tag on a stolen GMC pickup carried the same number on different backgrounds, so the camera could not tell them apart. This is a system used outside the conditions it was built for, because it was matching a character string that was never unique to one vehicle.

The failure surfaced at the point where an alert becomes a police stop. In Colwich, Kansas, a Flock alert led to the Spurlocks being stopped, and police found the duplicate number and said the wrong plate type was entered. A month later in Catoosa, Oklahoma, another alert led officers to stop them at a casino, where officers drew guns and handcuffed Matthew before learning the mistake. Wichita police Captain Casey Slaughter said a Flock alert alone is not enough for a stop, but a wrong plate type entry can still lead to action. Catching this before the stop would have required checking the plate type or background against the record, which the camera does not read, or a human confirmation step between the alert and the officers' response.

It is not established who or what entered the wrong plate type, or whether the stops followed department policy. The account comes from a single outlet's investigation, and a report is not a finding of fault. Kansas has over 100 plate designs, about half specialty, and is moving from six digit to seven digit numbers to avoid duplicates. The Spurlocks' stolen plate entry has expired, so they no longer expect stops.

Matthew and Leah Spurlock have a KU Alumni plate numbered 7007. Kansas reuses numbers on different plate designs, and a stolen GMC pickup had a temporary Kansas tag with the same number but a different background. In Colwich, Kansas, a Flock camera alerted police, and the Spurlocks were stopped. Police found the duplicate number and said the wrong plate type was entered. A month later, in Catoosa, Oklahoma, another Flock camera led police to stop them at a casino. Officers drew guns and handcuffed Matthew before learning the mistake.

Wichita police Captain Casey Slaughter said Flock cameras read only letters and numbers, not plate backgrounds, so they cannot tell specialty plates apart. He said a Flock alert alone is not enough for a stop, but a wrong plate type entry can still lead to action. Kansas has over 100 plate designs, about half specialty, and is moving from six digit to seven digit numbers to avoid duplicates. The Spurlocks' stolen plate entry has expired, so they no longer expect stops. They hope to keep their 14 year old plate.
